Very intersting read: Nick Cammarata, a co-author of the 2020 Zoom In paper that introduced the idea that neural networks fold unrelated concepts into the same neurons, now says the field misread its own key evidence. In an essay published Thursday by interpretability startup Goodfire, he reports that in a preliminary audit of Qwen3-32B, roughly 90% of neuron signals have one main job and only 2-4% are not yet understood; the automated study he started at OpenAI in 2023 judged about 1.7% legible with the tools of the time.

After all, let’s remember: According to OpenAI’s own System Card, GPT-6 Astra's reasoning is harder to monitor than that of its predecessors. According to The Information, the next model is expected to rely on Loop Transformers, which think more in numbers and less in readable text.

That sounds like a solution: if the text disappears, you just look inside. However, this is still far from being a viable real-time monitoring method, and the testing was conducted on classic transformers, not on loop architectures. Still, it's a good step in the right direction and can be a great help in understanding the system, and thus in ensuring its safety.

Crazy that most people missed that but Google has demonstrated a quantum computing breakthrough that could bring complex chemistry and materials simulations closer to practical use.

On its Willow processor, researchers report producing essential quantum states with around 40× lower error than preparation without “magic state cultivation,” reaching approximately 99.99% fidelity.
These states are consumed during computation. Producing enough reliable ones is one of the biggest resource bottlenecks in building useful, error-corrected quantum computers.

Google has now demonstrated on hardware a method designed to reduce that problem.

For science, the potential is very very significant: calculating how electrons interact in complex molecules and materials, helping researchers investigate chemical reactions, catalysts and properties that remain difficult to model accurately with classical computers.

The main thing I notice AIs do that humans don't is write lots of scripts running searches and verifications.

They don't work in a small search space, and they aren't using a gigabrain directly on a large search space. They're just writing lots of scripts to search large spaces that would be annoying to do.

When I watch them work, I mostly think, "Oh I probably should've been doing that. But I'm just so lazy, I would never crank out 1000 lines of Python doing a bunch of Grobner basis or group theory calculations just to test a hypothesis." Even if it would've been more reliable and less work overall.

Your computer runs billions of clock cycles per second, and AIs will actually use it for thinking.

I also think: If math had "industrial value", then this would've been systematized and you could train people to search for math solutions like an AI. Maybe Bel is superhuman, but lots of people could be an Astra if the computational approaches were written down and taught.

It's the difference between "stare at a paper, think, hope a pattern comes to mind" vs. "What is a good search space? Let me feed that into an SMT solver or CAS or custom C++ searcher." Of course, many people do that, but not as fluently and consistently as AI.

More from Nick:

wow, amazing technical blog post about microsoft's new 3T pre-training with very rare and clear insights on how to train models of this size

first let's get an overview of the shape of this model, it's a sparser model than Kimi K3 (80B active vs 104B), same sliding window hybrid pattern, with this time more kv heads for the sliding window layers (a bit different from stepfun and poolside that add query head). they added a shared expert and also removed the interleaved MoE/Dense pattern of MAI 1

the scaling ladder is very similar to MAI 1 with the same mechanism, each rung depends only on the number of layers. they mention that one of the key improvements is how they handle the smaller rung data distribution where they make sure to have the same repetition as the final corpus. they already did that for MAI-1 but only for data ablation iirc

their prediction is almost identical to the final run loss, very impressive

they compare the model with different base models such as deepseek v4 pro and MAI 1, tho in the case of deepseek v4 pro i'd say it's quite hard to distinguish how much the data mixture "overfitting" to the scaling ladder has an impact here (they mention it's both), need to always be a bit careful about EG metrics for data in general

they have VERY NICE scaling laws for weight decay and learning rate, for the learning rate they express it as a function of tokens per parameter (N/D) and steps (hence depending on the batch size). they also do the same for dropout where it's a function of active params only, they also find the usual sqrt(k) scaling for learning rate and batch size (other scaling laws often also converge to that)

a bunch of other stability stuff, they use Muon this time and activation gradient clipping, the efficiency gain here is actually pretty crazy at larger scale. they also increase the training horizon to ~40T text (20T unique) + a new 10T (4.5T unique) multimodal  since the model is natively multimodal

imo this is a safe but very clean scaling! very exciting for the tech report and MAI-base-3, congrats!!

We're expanding access to GPT-Rosalind for academic research.

The new Rosalind Academic Plan helps scientific labs bring AI into the work of understanding biology, exploring ideas, and deciding what to test next—with sponsored access for eligible labs at U.S. universities.

Academic research starts with questions whose impact may take years to impact human health.

GPT-Rosalind is built to support that work: helping researchers reason across scientific literature and biological data, with scientists bringing the expertise and judgment to evaluate the evidence.

Eligible labs can receive up to 12 months of sponsored access to OpenAI tools, with GPT-Rosalind access subject to trusted-access approval.

Research data shared through the Rosalind Academic Plan is not used to train our models by default.

Last week, Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Florida Panhandle. Our thoughts are with everyone affected and with the recovery efforts still underway. Earlier and more accurate forecasting can help protect communities by giving them more time to prepare, and we are grateful that Google’s WeatherNext model was able to assist the @NWSNHC 's expert forecasters.

Based on initial evaluations, here's how our model supported the response to #Isaias:

- Tracking the Hurricane’s Path: WeatherNext was the most accurate model on the storm’s track. While traditional physics models predicted landfall closer to New Orleans, WeatherNext correctly predicted a path further east. This allowed NHC forecasters to highlight the potential for wind and storm surge impacts in the Florida Panhandle from their very first forecast. 

- More Time to Prepare: Up to three days before landfall, our model consistently predicted its eventual location in the Florida Panhandle to within 60 km or less, supporting the NHC as they honed in on a track toward the Florida Panhandle and issued hurricane watches and warnings to give officials in Florida, Alabama, and Mississippi more time to prepare. 

- Early Indications about Intensity: Early on, WeatherNext accurately predicted the intensification to a major hurricane. Alongside the regional hurricane models HWRF and HMON, WeatherNext’s intensity forecasts helped NHC forecasters to predict that the Isaias would approach the coast as a category 2 hurricane from the very first advisory. 

Giving communities more time and more accurate warnings is critical for protecting lives and livelihoods. While model performance varies from storm to storm, Isaias reflects our broader findings. In our recent @Nature paper co-authored with NHC forecasters, evaluating 200+ global tropical cyclones, we found our model provides ~1 day of additional lead time for both track and intensity.

It’s been an honor for the @GoogleDeepMind and @GoogleResearch teams to work alongside NHC forecasters. By combining AI, physics models, satellite data, and the crucial expertise of meteorologists, we're excited to keep pushing the boundaries of forecasting to help protect communities.

I am proud to share that SynthID has been recognised by @TIME as one of the Best Inventions of 2026.

When we first began developing this technology @GoogleDeepMind, the goal was to find a robust, imperceptible way to watermark AI-generated media directly at the moment of creation, without compromising content quality.

It was no small research challenge. But three years into its use, SynthID has already watermarked over 180 billion images and videos, alongside 240,000 years of audio. We’ve also recently extended these watermarking principles to biology with SynthID Bio.

SynthID isn't a silver bullet for misinformation and this isn't a challenge any one company can solve alone; but it does represent a step toward a more transparent information ecosystem.

A sincere thank you to the teams across @Google for their contributions to making SynthID a reality, and also for the support the team has received from @demishassabis, @sundarpichai  and the rest of the Google leadership on this journey.
